title: Diesel Is in Your P&L, Whether You Buy It or Not
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell argues that CEOs outside the energy sector should treat the record diesel crack spread as a leadership signal rather than someone else's problem. Citing Apollo economist Torsten Slok, he explains that diesel costs move through freight, supplier pricing and eventually core inflation, with a lag that makes the exposure easy to miss. He walks through the three constituencies a CEO must balance, customers, employees and shareholders, and shows how the same shock pulls on all three at once. Practical moves include tracing where diesel enters the cost structure, deciding a pricing posture before the first increase lands, modelling a higher-compensation case, and rerunning capital decisions against a higher cost of money. He is explicit that the goal is to put ranges around the risk rather than to predict where diesel will trade. The piece closes with a question about whether the leadership team would already know what to do if costs rose next quarter.
points: The lag between an energy shock and its appearance in your P&L is a window of opportunity, because supplier surcharges and contract renewals delay the pain.
Trace exposure one level deeper than usual by asking where diesel hides in freight, packaging, maintenance, field service and vendor costs.
Decide your pricing posture before the first big increase arrives, and talk with your largest customers early so a price change is a business conversation rather than an invoice surprise.
Rerun any capital commitment approved under lower rate assumptions, since the 10-year Treasury above 5 percent changes acquisition, expansion and refinancing math.
Use ranges and scenarios instead of forecasts: the useful exercise is knowing which decisions change if costs stay high.
quotes: A diesel shock does not appear in your P&L all at once. Some suppliers will absorb higher freight costs for a while. Others have fuel surcharges that reset periodically.
That delay can make the problem easy to miss. The economics underneath your vendors can be changing for months before anything obvious changes in your own numbers.
Raise prices too quickly or too broadly and you may give a competitor an opening. Wait too long and you can give away margin that will be difficult to recover later.
And if an increase looks likely, talk with your largest customers early. A price change discussed as part of a business conversation is very different from one discovered on an invoice.
You do not need to change the budget today. You should know what you would change if the assumptions behind it do.
None of those questions requires you to know where diesel will trade next March. They require you to know which decisions inside your company become different if it stays expensive.
Part of the CEO’s job is maintaining enough distance from today’s operating problems to notice the forces that may alter the next quarter or the next year.
